topics.name: Past tenses in a story (simple, continuous, perfect)
Reported speech with say, tell and ask

questions.prompt: Pick the sentence with the correct tense.
options: One night a man had a dream.
One night a man was have a dream.
One night a man haved a dream.
questions.rule: A finished past event uses the simple past. The past of have is had.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the semicolon correctly?
options: Cyril kept; asking questions as his aunt had no answers.
Cyril kept asking questions; his aunt had no answers.
Cyril kept asking questions; because his aunt had no answers.
questions.rule: A semicolon joins two complete, closely linked sentences. It never splits a verb, and is not used before because.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Both the girls is plural, so the past continuous uses were: were asking.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Third conditional result: would have + past participle: would have stayed.
the ... ever compares with all others, so use the superlative: the best.

questions.after: the children a story about Bertha.
questions.rule: We tell someone a story. Said and spoke cannot take a person + a story after them.

questions.prompt: Describe the scene in the past continuous.
questions.rule: Past continuous: was + -ing for an action going on in the past: was sniffing.

chat: Is your sister older than you?
options: No, she is more young than me.
No, she is younger than me.
No, she is youngest than me.
questions.rule: Short adjectives add -er before than: younger than.

options: Cyril said that I was bored.
Cyril said that he were bored.
Cyril said that he was bored.
questions.rule: I becomes he for Cyril, and am moves back to was.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 2 errors in this paragraph.
questions.rule: The story is in the past: were bored and kept asking. After to, use the base verb: to tell.

options: If the aunt had told a better story, the children will have listened.
If the aunt has told a better story, the children would have listened.
If the aunt had told a better story, the children would have listened.
questions.rule: Third conditional: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle.

options: The aunt said that the story was very good.
The aunt told that the story was very good.
The aunt said me that the story was very good.
questions.rule: Say needs no person after it: said that. Tell needs a person: told me that.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: Comparing with all the others needs the superlative: the most obedient.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: The earlier action takes the past perfect (had flashed); the later one takes the simple past: looked.
An action going on when another past action happened takes the past continuous: was hiding.
A reported order: asked + person + to + base verb: asked Cyril to sit down.

chat: Oh no, we missed the school bus this morning!
options: If we had left early, we would have catch it.
If we had left early, we would have caught it.
If we left early, we would have caught it.
questions.rule: For an unreal past: If + had left, would have caught.

chat: Why didn't you answer my call?
options: Sorry, Ma. I am travelling on the train yesterday.
Sorry, Ma. I was travelling on the train.
Sorry, Ma. I was travel on the train.
questions.rule: An action in progress at a past moment takes the past continuous: I was travelling.

questions.source: The girl said to the bachelor, "Tell us a story."
options: The girl asked the bachelor to tell us a story.
The girl asked the bachelor to tell them a story.
The girl asked the bachelor to told them a story.
questions.rule: An order becomes asked + person + to + base verb, and us becomes them.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 2 errors in this paragraph.
questions.rule: The ... ever heard needs the superlative best. The pattern is as good as, never as good than.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the colon correctly?
options: Bertha had: three medals for obedience, punctuality and good behaviour.
Bertha had three medals: one for obedience, one for punctuality and one for good behaviour.
Bertha won three medals for: obedience, punctuality and good behaviour.
questions.rule: A colon comes after a complete statement to introduce a list. It never comes straight after a verb or a preposition.

options: If Bertha hadn't worn the medals, the wolf wouldn't have found her.
If Bertha hasn't worn the medals, the wolf wouldn't have found her.
If Bertha hadn't worn the medals, the wolf won't have found her.
questions.rule: Third conditional: If + hadn't worn, wouldn't have found.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: When the listener is named, use tell: told his aunt that. Said needs to before a person.

questions.after: bored long before the aunt started her story.
questions.rule: The earlier of two past actions takes the past perfect: had become ... before she started.

questions.before: If the wolf had not heard the medals, Bertha
questions.rule: The result of an unreal past: would have + past participle: would have survived.

questions.prompt: Join two ideas with a semicolon.
questions.rule: A semicolon joins two complete, closely linked ideas: The story was dull; nobody listened.

chat: What did the bus conductor tell you?
options: He told me that the bus will left at six.
He told me that the bus would leave at six.
He said me that the bus would leave at six.
questions.rule: Told + person + that; will leave moves back to would leave.

chat: Which story did you like more?
options: The second one. It was far exciting than the first.
The second one. It was far more exciting than the first.
The second one. It was far most exciting than the first.
questions.rule: Long adjectives use more + adjective + than; far makes it stronger: far more exciting than.

questions.source: The bachelor's story was the most exciting story of all.
options: The bachelor's story was more exciting than any other story.
The bachelor's story was more exciting than any story.
The bachelor's story was most exciting than any other story.
questions.rule: Superlative to comparative: more exciting than any other. Without other, the story is compared with itself.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 2 errors in this paragraph.
questions.rule: Third conditional: would have + past participle (caught) and if + had + past participle (had not trembled).

options: Bertha had hid in the bushes before the wolf reached them.
Bertha has hidden in the bushes before the wolf reached them.
Bertha had hidden in the bushes before the wolf reached them.
questions.rule: Past perfect = had + past participle. The past participle of hide is hidden.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: A reported request: asked + person + to + base verb: to come and listen.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: With would have invited, the if-clause needs the past perfect: If Bertha had been.

questions.before: No other child in the town had
questions.rule: Medals can be counted, so use as many ... as. Much is for uncountable nouns.
If + had + past participle, would have + past participle.

chat: What did the ticket checker ask you?
options: He asked me where I was going.
He asked me where was I going.
He asked me where am I going.
questions.rule: A reported question uses statement order and moves the tense back: where I was going.

chat: Why were you late for practice?
options: By the time I reached the station, the train has already left.
By the time I reached the station, the train had already left.
By the time I reach the station, the train had already left.
questions.rule: The earlier past action takes the past perfect (had left); the later one takes the simple past (reached).

questions.source: The bachelor said to the aunt, "I don't agree with you."
options: The bachelor told the aunt that he doesn't agree with you.
The bachelor told the aunt that he didn't agree with her.
The bachelor told the aunt that he didn't agreed with her.
questions.rule: said to becomes told; don't moves back to didn't + base verb; I/you become he/her.

questions.source: The aunt did not tell a good story. So the children did not listen.
options: If the aunt told a good story, the children would have listened.
If the aunt had told a good story, the children would listen.
If the aunt had told a good story, the children would have listened.
questions.rule: Imagining a different past: If + had told, would have listened.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 2 errors in this paragraph.
questions.rule: Told needs a listener; with no listener use a verb like added that. After to, use the base verb: to continue.

options: Had Bertha not wore her medals, the wolf would never have found her.
Had Bertha not worn her medals, the wolf would never have found her.
Had Bertha not worn her medals, the wolf would never had found her.
questions.rule: Had + subject + past participle can replace If: Had Bertha not worn ..., would never have found.

questions.prompt: One word is wrong. Find it and fix it.
questions.rule: When we compare only two people, we use the comparative: the taller one.

questions.after: in the bush for a few minutes when the medals clinked.
questions.rule: An action that had gone on for some time before a past event takes the past perfect continuous: had been hiding.

questions.after: the train earlier, the children would have troubled him even more.
questions.rule: The result would have troubled needs the past perfect in the if-clause: had not left.
A reported yes/no question: asked whether + statement order; was moves back to had been.

chat: You lost the semi-final. What went wrong?
options: If I had practised harder, I would have won it.
If I had practised harder, I would won it.
If I would have practised harder, I would have won it.
questions.rule: Never put would in the if-clause. Use If I had practised, I would have won.

questions.source: "Were there any sheep in the park?" demanded Cyril.
options: Cyril asked whether were there any sheep in the park.
Cyril asked whether there have been any sheep in the park.
Cyril asked whether there had been any sheep in the park.
questions.rule: A yes/no question takes whether + statement order; were moves back to had been.

questions.source: Bertha was the best child in the town.
options: No other child in the town was so good than Bertha.
No other child in the town was as good as Bertha.
No other child in the town was as better as Bertha.
questions.rule: Superlative to positive: No other ... as good as. The positive degree uses the plain adjective.

questions.prompt: Rewrite as one sentence using a semicolon.
questions.source: The wolf could not see Bertha. The myrtle bushes were too thick.
options: The wolf could not see Bertha; the myrtle bushes were too thick.
The wolf could not see Bertha; because the myrtle bushes were too thick.
The wolf could not see Bertha: and the myrtle bushes were too thick.
questions.rule: A semicolon alone joins two closely linked sentences; it is not followed by because or and.

questions.prompt: Find and fix the 3 errors in this paragraph.
questions.rule: Tell a past story in the past: came, ran. After would have, use the past participle: gone.
